title: Air-gap transmission lines by sacrificial polymer release
idea: Reverse 'more dielectric': pattern interposer signal lines on a sacrificial polymer (e.g. polynorbornene) and thermally decompose it through a porous cap, leaving copper lines suspended in air (k~1) instead of polyimide (k~3.3).
why: CV^2 link energy (facts 5, 10): line capacitance roughly halves, giving ~2x lower energy and faster interposer memory links with spin, pattern and bake steps only.

title: Antibody tags: send a fingerprint instead of an already-known line
idea: The HBM base die and the host controller each keep an 'immune memory' of hashes of recently transferred 64 B lines. When a requested line matches a hash the host already holds, the stack sends a 16-bit antibody tag and the host rebuilds the line from its own scratchpad, with a full-transfer fallback on mismatch. Zero lines, duplicated KV-cache blocks and repeated weight tiles become near-free transfers.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and effective bandwidth: in dedup-heavy AI and VM workloads, 15-40% of transfers could collapse to tags, cutting link energy and freeing bandwidth.

title: Charge-recycling bus: stacked voltage domains reuse every transition
idea: Invert 'each bit transition dumps its charge to ground': split the bus into N series-stacked voltage domains so charge discharging a line in domain k charges a line in domain k-1, with a small balancing regulator closing the loop.
why: Cuts I/O CV2 energy roughly by N (2-4x) despite the ~1 V floor, attacking the voltage floor and data-movement energy.

title: IBM EL-1 revival: maskless e-beam RDL in non-fluorinated PMMA resist
idea: Revive IBM's 1970s EL-1 direct-write e-beam personalization: multi-beam writers pattern interposer RDL and base-die customization layers directly in PMMA or HSQ, with no PFAS photoacid generators, giving per-product memory interface variants without masks.
why: Constraint: removes chemically amplified resists with PFAS PAGs; capital: no $1-5M mask sets for low-volume custom HBM base dies and interposers, and throughput suffices for a few coarse layers.

title: Thin films: chip-on-film display lines make flexible memory ribbons
idea: TRIZ #30 Flexible shells and thin films: reuse display-driver chip-on-film lines (~18 um pitch on polyimide) to make flexible memory ribbons. LPDDR dies on flex tape are bonded to the package edge and folded up around the cold plate, adding capacity in 3D without using board area. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity per package and data movement (fact 5): ~2x more LPDDR per accelerator at ~2-4 pJ/bit, using idle COF capacity.

title: Kaleidoscope: link-level cache-line dedup dictionary at both ends
idea: Like a kaleidoscope's repeated patterns: small matched dictionaries at the memory controller and in the CXL device remember recently sent 64B lines, and a repeated line crosses the link as a 10-bit index. Prototyped in FPGA RTL.
why: Link bandwidth and pJ/bit: 1.3-2x effective bandwidth on zero-heavy or duplicate-heavy traffic.

title: Ship high-order bits, predict the rest on arrival
idea: Substitute full-precision transfers with split-significance links: only sign, exponent and top mantissa bits of BF16/FP8 activations cross by default; a tiny per-tensor predictor fills low bits from local statistics and exact low bits are fetched lazily for sensitive layers.
why: Facts 5/8: ~40-50% fewer bits per value moved; effective HBM bandwidth up 1.6-2x.

title: Bit-plane progressive fetch stops when precision suffices
idea: Eliminate low-order bits from the bus: store tensors transposed into bit-planes and fetch sign/exponent/MSB planes first; the consumer's datapath signals 'enough' as soon as the result (e.g., top-k ordering or a dot-product bound) can no longer change, and the remaining planes are never sent.
why: Data movement is 20-25% of accelerator power: on LLM decode ~40-60% of mantissa bits are provably unnecessary per operation, cutting bytes moved ~1.5-2x without fixed quantization loss.

title: Thermal hysteresis: NiTi shape-memory microcontacts make HBM stacks reworkable
idea: Replace permanent microbumps with NiTi micro-springs that clamp pads at operating temperature and release when the stack is heated through the austenite transition, so one failed DRAM die in a 12-high stack is lifted out and replaced instead of scrapping the stack and its GPU.
why: HBM compound yield and scrap (fact 6): converts a $1,000+ package loss into a single-die swap; contact resistance and ~20 um pitch limit it.

title: Graceful capacity decay: code rate grows as modules age
idea: Stretch the memory's timescale to a decade: the base die tracks raw BER as cells wear and leak (up to 1% and beyond), automatically raising parity and announcing a slightly lower capacity through a hot-capacity-change event the OS honors. Modules retire only when ~15% capacity is gone.
why: Roughly doubles service life of deployed DRAM/HBM, effectively adding supply, and lets new parts ship with thinner margins.

title: Air-gap suspended interposer wires: vacuum dielectric instead of oxide
idea: Substitute the oxide/polyimide around long interposer lines with air: a sacrificial polynorbornene layer is thermally decomposed after RDL build, leaving copper lines suspended on periodic posts and cutting line capacitance ~3x.
why: Fact 5/10: wire CV^2 drops ~60%, taking the interconnect share of HBM energy from ~3-4 toward ~1.5-2 pJ/bit.

title: YBCO superconducting interposer lines at 77 K
idea: MINIFY line loss to near zero: pattern YBCO superconducting traces on a sapphire interposer, cool the package with liquid nitrogen, and let memory sit centimeters away with lossless, low-swing transmission.
why: Data-movement energy: link energy limited only by drivers (~0.05 pJ/bit); cold DRAM also cuts leakage and refresh.

title: Air-gap interposer wiring cuts per-bit wire capacitance
idea: Eliminate the dielectric between HBM-to-GPU interposer lines: after patterning, selectively etch a sacrificial polymer to leave lines suspended in air (k~1 vs ~3.5) on periodic support posts, then seal with a cap layer.
why: On-interposer link energy is dominated by wire capacitance: ~3x lower C gives ~2-3x lower pJ/bit and permits longer reach, so more stacks can surround one GPU.

title: Air-gap interposer wires halve memory link capacitance
idea: Po: the best insulator is nothing. One mask defines where a sacrificial fill between interposer lines is later removed, leaving air gaps around long HBM-to-GPU wires.
why: Wire capacitance falls 2-3x, so CV2 energy on interposer links drops the same amount; ~1.5 pJ/bit saved on 3-4 pJ/bit HBM links.

title: Charge-recycling stacked-voltage memory bus at 50 mV swing
idea: Worsen: swing every link wire rail-to-rail at 1.1 V and dump the charge to ground. Flip: stack link lanes in series voltage domains so the charge one lane releases on a transition becomes the next lane's supply, and run interposer lines at ~50-100 mV differential swing into sense-amp receivers.
why: CV^2 wall on links (facts 5, 10): 5-10x lower link energy, moving HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.4 pJ/bit.

title: Si: deep-trench DRAM built into the passive interposer itself
idea: Interposers are thousands of mm2 of idle silicon: fabricate 1T1C eDRAM in them using the deep-trench capacitors (~30-60 fF, far above the ~5 fF pillar wall) that interposer lines already offer for decoupling, at 65-90 nm DUV rules, as a memory tier beside the HBM stacks.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and capital (fact 4): a 2,500 mm2 interposer could add ~1-2 GB of low-latency memory on fully depreciated DUV tools; large Cs also relaxes refresh.

title: Gutenberg movable-type interposer from standard bridge pieces
idea: Keep a catalog of pre-made standard silicon bridge tiles (memory-PHY, power, crossbar), the way a printer keeps metal type, and compose each product's interposer from them in a molded frame. No new interposer masks are needed per product.
why: Cuts the mask, NRE and lead time of custom interposers (weeks instead of months) and frees CoWoS capacity for more HBM attach.

title: Dual-ported HBM stack serving two GPU chiplets
idea: Po: the memory has two front doors. One added redistribution mask on the base die creates a second bump field on the opposite edge, so one stack sits between two GPU chiplets and both read the same data without copies.
why: Shared weights and KV cache need no duplicate copy; effective capacity per GPU pair up 30-50%.

title: Ephemeral-memory cloud SKU: cheap RAM that forgets after 50 ms
idea: Ideal: users pay only for memory during the instant they use it. Closest achievable: a cloud instance class exposes a large never-refreshed 'ephemeral memory' region whose contents are guaranteed only 50 ms after the last write, priced ~40% lower, with SDKs for streaming ETL, video, AI activations and network buffers that fit the contract.
why: Zero refresh power on the ephemeral tier, and providers can fill it with DRAM dies that fail standard retention bins, salvaging 5-10% more usable supply from existing output.

title: Auto-parts remanufacturing for HBM: harvest, re-bump, redeploy stacks
idea: Adapted from the alternator/starter core-return model: HBM stacks from retired accelerators are thermally debonded, tested, re-bumped and mounted on CXL memory cards or low-cost interposers for inference and cache tiers.
why: Raises usable supply with no wafers: each retired 8-GPU node holds ~1-1.5 TB of HBM that is now shredded; reclaiming half adds supply at near-zero capital.

title: Weaverbird woven interposer: copper and glass-fiber threads loomed into substrate
idea: Weaverbirds knot strong nests from simple strands. Memory-module substrates are woven on modified textile looms from insulated copper microwires and glass optical fibers, warp-weft crossings are laser-welded where vias are needed, and the cloth is resin-impregnated before DRAM packages are mounted.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: cheap domestic looms make high-capacity CXL memory boards with built-in optics at a fraction of PCB/HDI tooling cost.

title: 3D-printed micro-spring sockets for test-then-stack dies
idea: Substitute tungsten-rhenium probe needles and permanent bonds with two-photon-printed polymer micro-springs metallized by electroless plating, forming sockets that contact bare-die pads for at-speed known-good-die test and temporary mounting.
why: Fact 6 yield and the tungsten chokepoint: test-before-stack recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss and removes W probe dependence.

title: DSL-on-old-copper: multi-tone HBM over plain organic substrate
idea: DSL got broadband out of old phone wire. Use DMT/OFDM multi-tone signaling, with bits loaded per tone, on cm-long traces in organic substrate. Wide memory stacks then connect with no silicon interposer or bridge.
why: CoWoS-class silicon interposers are a capacity chokepoint and a cost driver. Organic memory links at ~1-2 pJ/bit could cut package cost 30-50% and free HBM-class bandwidth from interposer supply.

title: LED-lithography coarse wiring paired with ultra-wide slow low-swing bus
idea: Combine 365 nm UV-LED array exposure (solid-state: no Hg-Ar/Xe lamp, no neon excimer), which only patterns ~2-5 um lines, with an interface designed for that limit: 8-16k parallel interposer wires at 0.5-1 Gb/s, 100-150 mV swing, no SerDes or DLL, delivering TB/s from coarse wiring.
why: Data movement and capital: ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM, with interposers made in PCB-class fabs; the constraint becomes the design driver.

title: lossy_malloc: cloud memory tier priced by tolerated bit error rate
idea: Create a datacenter-scale market: the allocator exposes lossy_malloc(ber=1e-2), mapping those pages onto pools with 1%-BER cells, B-grade dies or relaxed refresh at ~1/3 the price, and frameworks place embeddings, KV caches and media buffers there by default.
why: Creates demand for cheap error-tolerant capacity, multiplying usable supply for AI and media without new fabs.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops tiny DRAM dielets into panel wells
idea: Box: 0.5 mm2 DRAM dielets x standard x on-dielet SA x shape-keyed wells plus panel RDL x 600 mm organic panel x fluidic self-assembly. Asymmetric trapezoid dielets tumble in a carrier fluid until they lock into matching wells, then one RDL pass wires thousands of dielets into wide memory channels.
why: Yield and assembly capital: tiny dies yield >95% even at aggressive rules, and parallel assembly replaces millions of pick-and-place moves; cost per good bit -15-25%.

title: Potter's kiln: co-fired AlN ceramic memory brick with copper lines
idea: Fired ceramics last millennia: co-fire an aluminium nitride carrier with copper conductors (no tungsten) to form a 'memory brick' that holds 4-8 DRAM dies around a logic die, with a silicon-matched CTE (~4.5 ppm/K) and 170 W/mK conductivity.
why: A rugged 125 C/10 year memory module that avoids China-dominated tungsten and organic laminates, with less thermal-cycle stress than FR-4.

title: Electricity spot market for rack-scale memory capacity and bandwidth
idea: Adapted from wholesale power markets with 5-minute nodal pricing: CXL-pooled memory in a cluster is auctioned in short intervals. Jobs bid for capacity and bandwidth, and lightly loaded servers sell their stranded DRAM back into the pool.
why: Raises usable supply by monetizing idle DRAM (typical utilization 40-60%); ~15-30% less DRAM purchased per cluster.

title: Standard-gauge memory chiplet footprint like ISO shipping containers
idea: Publish a CHIPS-funded open standard bump map, PHY and stack height for memory chiplets so any domestic DRAM, MRAM or gain-cell die slots onto any base die, the way ISO containers made intermodal shipping work.
why: Creates a second-source market for memory, lowers entry barriers for U.S. makers, and raises supply elasticity.

title: Continuity: wide-IO DRAM redesigned for fully depreciated legacy DRAM lines
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: keep retiring 2x/3x-nm DRAM lines running by taping out a new 512-bit-wide, low-speed DRAM die for them, designed for fan-out packaging beside accelerators. The wide, slow interface hides the older node's lower density. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital (fact 4): depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, so fully depreciated lines make bits at about half the wafer cost, adding supply with zero new fab capex.

title: Alien sees silicon as glass: through-die infrared vertical links
idea: To an alien eye silicon is transparent at 1310 nm. Stack thinned dies with no TSVs and talk vertically with Ge-on-Si micro-photodiodes and tiny modulated emitters or reflectors aimed straight through the silicon bulk, with alignment set by bonding registration.
why: Removes signal TSVs entirely (only power vias remain), so each die gets denser and stack yield rises; dense 10 um optical 'vias' at ~0.2 pJ/bit.

title: Piggy bank: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn on CXL expander cards
idea: The 'piggy bank' of savings is the DDR4 sitting in decommissioned servers. Design a PCIe/CXL card around an off-the-shelf CXL memory controller ASIC that hosts 8 used DDR4 RDIMMs, plus a burn-in and test flow, and sell it as a capacity tier. Board design and pilot runs fit within $1M.
why: Cost per bit and supply: reused bits cost roughly 10-20% of new DDR5 and need zero new wafers.

title: Voyager engineer's lane sparing with lifetime eye-margin remapping
idea: Voyager has run for 49 years on redundancy: add 10% spare lanes, have the base die measure every lane's eye margin weekly and move traffic off lanes that are degrading before they fail, keeping a wear map in on-die fuses.
why: Turns 10 year/125 C bump and TSV wear-out from a fatal event into graceful degradation, which allows fewer, finer-pitch lanes without needing big margins.

title: Mat-granular bond clusters for 64-byte, zero-overfetch activation
idea: Ideal: fetch exactly the byte asked for and nothing else. Closest achievable: give every 512x512 mat its own cluster of hybrid-bond pads for local wordline enable and data, so the logic die activates a single mat segment instead of an 8 KB page spread across 16 mats.
why: Fact 8 overfetch: 128x overfetch falls to ~8x and random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.6 pJ; fewer cells disturbed per ACT also eases row hammer (fact 9).

title: Shingled LPDDR staircase on glass panel replaces TSV stacks
idea: Box: 1T1C LPDDR die x planar access x on-die SA x offset-staircase edge pads x glass-core panel x panel-level RDL. Eight LPDDR dies are shingled with 0.4 mm offsets so every die's edge pads stay exposed, then a single panel-level RDL plus through-glass vias wires all eight to a 1024-bit bus without one TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area and no 20-30% stack yield loss; uses commodity LPDDR wafers at roughly half the wafer area per bit of HBM, at about half HBM's bandwidth density.

title: N: GaN micro-LED arrays form a wide-slow optical memory bus
idea: Bond 1,000-element GaN micro-LED emitter arrays and Si photodiode arrays to the memory controller and to a remote DRAM sled, each LED running 2-4 Gb/s NRZ into one core of an imaging fiber bundle, so the bus stays massively parallel and protocol-light like HBM instead of serializing.
why: Data movement (fact 5): sub-1 pJ/bit over 1-10 m with no SerDes or lasers, letting HBM-class bandwidth come from cheap off-package DRAM and avoiding the HBM TSV tax per accelerator.

title: B-grade die recapture: weak-cell DRAM fallout into heavy-ECC stacks
idea: Move the pass/fail line from zero unrepairable bits to <=1% weak cells: dies that fab test would scrap or down-bin are stacked on a heavy-LDPC base die and sold as full-capacity memory, with a buyer contracting for fab fallout at scrap-plus prices.
why: Raises usable bit supply from existing wafers ~5-15% (typical DRAM yield loss) with zero new fab capex.

title: Micro-Velcro hook-and-loop reworkable memory die attach
idea: Plate copper mushroom hooks through i-line resist on one die and loop arrays on the other; pressing them interlocks hundreds of thousands of contacts at room temperature. A stack can be peeled off and swapped.
why: Reworkable stacks raise effective yield and enable field-upgradeable memory; no solder reflow and no EUV.

title: Marconi coherer revival: link receivers that latch arriving bits nonvolatilely
idea: Like the 1890s coherer whose filings fused under RF, end each die-to-die write lane with a filamentary Ag/Cu nanogap switch that forms a filament when a pulse arrives, so the receiver is itself a nonvolatile staging latch, reset later by a counter-pulse 'tapper'.
why: Facts 3/5: merges receiver and write buffer, removing an SRAM/register staging hop for write-mostly streams (checkpoints, KV-cache spill), ~30% data-path energy on those writes; endurance limits it to staging, not working memory.

title: Hot-stack: DRAM bonded straight onto a 1 kW GPU at 125 C
idea: Shift the thermal scale: retention collapses at high temperature, which is why DRAM is kept off hot logic, but with 1% tolerance and row-scale codes DRAM dies can be hybrid-bonded directly on the GPU die at 115-125 C with refresh only modestly raised.
why: Deletes the interposer and HBM PHY (facts 5, 6): memory-on-logic at ~0.1 pJ/bit in the tightest possible package.

title: Stadium-broadcast optical star coupler shares weights across 64 accelerators
idea: Broadcast TV sends one stream to millions of receivers. Keep one copy of model weights in a shared memory appliance whose optical output is split by a passive star coupler to 64 accelerators at once; each GPU's HBM holds only KV cache and activations while layers stream in lockstep.
why: Inference clusters store identical weights in every GPU's HBM; broadcasting removes 30-60% of per-GPU HBM capacity demand, directly stretching scarce HBM supply.

title: Selector-only memory fills TSV keep-out and PHY back-end areas
idea: Worsen: leave TSV keep-out zones and the space above PHYs as dead silicon. Flip: build stacked layers of chalcogenide selector-only memory (threshold set by write polarity, one two-terminal device per bit) in the BEOL above these regions, adding cross-point bits on area that today stores nothing.
why: Density from wasted area (facts 6, 7): ~20-30% of base and core die area gains 2-4 memory layers with no capacitor and no front-end steps.

title: Morse-code exponent coding on the memory link
idea: Morse gives frequent letters short codes. A tiny per-channel encoder in the HBM base die and the host PHY maps the highly skewed BF16/FP8 exponent fields to variable-length codes from a per-tensor table. Mantissas are sent raw.
why: Exponents hold only ~2-3 bits of entropy in 8 bits. Lossless coding cuts weight and activation traffic ~15-25%, with the same share of link energy saved.

title: Field-programmed antifuse stacks: burn weights through the memory interface
idea: Ideal: a memory you write once at deployment and never maintain. Closest achievable: multi-layer antifuse crosspoint dies (gate-oxide breakdown with diode select, 4F2 per layer) are programmed in place through the accelerator's own memory channels when a model is deployed, then served read-only with no refresh and no standby power.
why: Zero refresh and no per-model masks; stacked crosspoint OTP on mature nodes reaches DRAM-competitive density, and endurance is irrelevant for frozen weights.

title: Stalactite bonding: electroless copper grows across the gap
idea: Hold two dies face to face with a 2-5 um gap in an electroless copper bath; metal grows from both pads like stalactite and stalagmite until they fuse. No bonding force is needed.
why: Warp-tolerant, low-temperature stacking that preserves DRAM retention and lifts yield; parallel across whole wafers.

title: RFID fluidic self-assembly drops memory dielets into interposer wells
idea: Adapted from 1990s fluidic self-assembly used by RFID tag makers: millions of small DRAM dielets suspended in liquid flow over an interposer with etched, shape-matched wells. The dielets settle into place by gravity and shape and are then bonded by reflow.
why: Small dielets yield far better (yield ~ e^-AD), and assembly runs massively in parallel, cutting pick-and-place cost and large-die yield loss.

title: Refresh-piggybacked mirroring into a bonded non-volatile twin layer
idea: Eliminate the separate backup flush: a ferroelectric or MRAM twin layer bonded under each bank receives a row copy whenever that row is refreshed and its dirty bit is set (the row is already open, so only the vertical transfer is paid); at power loss only rows dirtied since their last refresh are flushed, within the PSU's existing ~10 ms hold-up energy.
why: Gives DRAM speed and endurance with full non-volatility, removing NVDIMM batteries/supercaps and 30-s serial flushes; copying rides on refresh activations, so no extra ACT energy or row-hammer exposure.

title: Endoscope imaging bundles carry microLED arrays for off-package HBM bandwidth
idea: Adapted from medical coherent fiber bundles with 10,000+ cores: a microLED array on the DRAM base die images straight into a bundle that lands on a photodiode array on the accelerator. The result is thousands of slow parallel lanes (~2 Gb/s each) with no lasers and no WDM.
why: Breaks interposer adjacency and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): HBM-class 2+ TB/s at ~1 pJ/bit over 1-10 m, so memory can live off-package in cheaper DDR-style dies.

title: Sense amplifiers reused as 50 mV link receivers
idea: MINIFY signal swing to ~50 mV by using the DRAM's own latch-type bitline sense-amplifier design (already built to resolve ~100 mV) as the receiver for low-swing differential links between DRAM and base die.
why: Voltage floor and pJ/bit: CV^2 energy on the link drops ~100x versus 0.4-0.5 V swing; claims ~0.05 pJ/bit inside the package.

title: Laser-free DRAM via retro-modulated light from host
idea: MINIFY the photonics on the memory side to passive reflective microring modulators: the host's comb laser sends continuous-wave light to the DRAM base die, which modulates and reflects it back on the same fiber.
why: Data movement and thermals: no laser or SerDes PLL on the DRAM side; claims <1 pJ/bit off-package links and a cooler, cheaper memory module.

title: Memory as master: the stack pushes tensors to compute
idea: Reverse who initiates: the host writes a descriptor program (tensor shapes, strides, schedule) once, and a DMA engine in the DRAM base die pushes data on its own schedule into the accelerator's SRAM over a write-only link; the host never issues per-line reads.
why: Removes request traffic and round-trip latency, and memory can order row activations optimally (fewer activations, less energy and row-hammer exposure); ~20% more effective bandwidth (facts 5, 8, 9).

title: Cable-TV head-end laser with polymer modulators on DRAM
idea: A cable head-end broadcasts a carrier to every home. Here a remote CW laser feeds light to the memory packages. The DRAM base die carries electro-optic polymer ring modulators (poled and cured ≤200 C) and sputtered low-temperature Ge photodetectors, so no laser or III-V growth enters the memory flow.
why: Optical memory links at <1 pJ/bit over meters allow disaggregated DRAM pools with no interposer. That cuts movement energy 3-10x against DDR5's 10-20 pJ/bit.

title: Laserless memory dies via optical backscatter modulation
idea: The irreducible optical cost is photons, not a laser on every die. The host sends continuous-wave light into the memory package; each DRAM base die carries only ring or electro-absorption modulators with a retroreflector, encoding read data onto reflected light like RFID backscatter, so the memory side spends ~10 fJ/bit and temperature-sensitive lasers stay at the host.
why: Optical memory links at ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit over meters let DRAM leave the hot accelerator package and decouple capacity from shoreline (facts 5, 6).

title: Logic on top, memory beneath through dedicated power columns
idea: Box: DRAM stack x standard x standard x power columns through reserved DRAM zones plus face-to-face signal bonds x DRAM as base x hybrid bonding. The accelerator die sits on top of the DRAM stack, next to the cold plate, and the DRAM below carries dedicated power-via columns, putting every compute tile ~50 um from its memory.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM shoreline: ~0.1 pJ/bit with bandwidth set by area rather than die edge; DRAM runs warmer, offset by temperature-aware refresh.

title: O: IGZO-TFT active glass interposer hosts memory buffers and repeaters
idea: Fabricate InGaZnO oxide thin-film transistors (display-fab tooling, 1-10 um rules) directly on a glass interposer to implement repeaters, address buffers, ECC and power gating between logic and many DRAM dies, so the DRAM base die/PHY shrinks and the memory plane can span half a meter.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7) and capital (fact 4): moves logic onto Gen-8 display tools at ~1/100 the $/mm2 of silicon; enables panel-sized memory planes with distributed repeaters.

title: MicroLED imaging-fiber links: each pixel a memory bit lane
idea: Ideal: thousands of wires with no wires. Closest achievable: put ~10,000 GaN microLEDs and silicon photodiodes on the DRAM base die, couple them into a coherent imaging fiber bundle and land it on a matching array on the GPU, each pixel carrying 2-4 Gb/s NRZ with no SerDes, lasers or modulators.
why: Fact 5: ~0.5-1 pJ/bit at metre reach with no retimers, so memory can leave the package and the interposer (fact 6) shrinks; no EUV and no III-V lasers needed.

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer's shingled staircase stack with overlap coupling
idea: Under embargo with no TSV etcher or interposer: shingle 8-16 thinned DRAM dies like roof tiles, each overlapping the one below by ~200 um, and pass signals through the overlap by capacitive proximity pads under 1 um of oxide, while power comes in by ordinary wire bonds on the exposed step.
why: Removes TSV drilling, CMP and fine-pitch bonder capex (fixes the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity), using wire-bond-era tools available in U.S. OSATs; ~1 Tb/s per stack at ~0.3 pJ/bit.

title: Co-extruded micro-coax ribbon cables for memory shelves
idea: Co-extrude polymer and copper (like making cable sheathing) into 50 um shielded micro-coax ribbons with 64 lanes each, terminated straight onto memory and compute packages. The low-loss, low-crosstalk path lets 30 cm links run near HBM energy.
why: PCB traces cost 5-10 pJ/bit; micro-coax claims ~1-2 pJ/bit at rack-shelf distances, enabling disaggregated memory without optics.

title: Bridge-resident row cache absorbs DRAM activations near GPU
idea: Box: 1T1C DRAM x standard access x on-DRAM SA x hybrid-bonded silicon bridge x Si bridge chiplet x 7 nm logic. The EMIB-style bridge between GPU and DRAM carries 64 MB of SRAM that holds whole recently opened 2 KB rows, fed through a 2 um-pitch hybrid bond so a full row moves for ~0.05 pJ/bit; re-hits are served from the bridge and the row is never re-activated.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8), row hammer (fact 9): 3-5x fewer activations on AI streams with reuse, random-read energy from ~5.9 to ~1.5 pJ per useful bit, and hammer patterns starve.

title: Zipper: sidewall hybrid bonds join DRAM and logic edge-to-edge
idea: Random word 'zipper' forced onto die edges: plasma-diced DRAM and logic dies get interdigitated comb-shaped sidewalls carrying Cu/oxide pads, then they are pushed together laterally and annealed so the teeth hybrid-bond like a zipper. Side-by-side dies then talk through edge bonds less than 100 um long, with no interposer and no silicon bridge.
why: Interposer/bridge cost and beachfront limit; lateral die-to-die links at ~0.1 pJ/bit vs ~0.5 pJ/bit on a 2.5D interposer, and CoWoS capacity drops out of the BOM.

title: Core-weaving revival: robots thread insulated microwire through laser-drilled stacks
idea: Like core-memory weavers threading wires through ferrite rings, laser-ablate aligned 20 um holes through a stack of thinned dies or glass and robotically thread polyester-imide-enamelled (not PTFE) copper microwire through them, then press-contact it to pads on each tier.
why: Constraint: laser ablation plus threading replaces Bosch DRIE, PFAS resists and plating chemistry for vertical interconnect; suited to 4-8-tier power/ground and slower signals at very low capital.

title: Ceiling MEMS free-space optics re-wire stranded rack DRAM per job phase
idea: Treat the datacenter ceiling as a memory backplane: MEMS steering mirrors link any compute sled to any memory sled with free-space optical beams, re-pointed in ~10 ms at job-phase boundaries that last seconds to minutes. DRAM stranded behind an idle CPU is lent to the busy GPU one row over.
why: Raises usable memory supply: 20-30% of datacenter DRAM is typically stranded, and recovering it is equivalent to new fab output with zero wafer capex.

title: Retired-server DRAM harvesting line feeding CXL expander cards
idea: Combine e-waste DIMM recovery with CXL memory expansion: an automated line desolders DDR4/DDR5 packages from retired DIMMs, reballs and characterizes each chip for retention and speed, bins them, and remounts them on CXL Type-3 cards whose controller maps weak rows and applies per-chip adaptive refresh. No new wafers, so no new rare gas.
why: Usable supply: millions of retired DIMMs per year become capacity at ~10-20% of new cost/bit during the shortage.

title: Refurbished-RAM trade died of test cost; PUF-certified reuse DRAM tier
idea: Secondary-market DRAM never scaled because per-module retest cost and counterfeit risk made buyers distrust it. Harvest DIMMs from decommissioned servers onto CXL expander cards whose controller runs full march and retention tests in situ and reads each die's retention-failure map as a physically unclonable fingerprint, issuing a signed provenance and health certificate, then sell the result as a 'certified reuse' capacity tier.
why: Raises usable memory supply with no new fab capital: millions of retired DIMMs a year re-enter service as a slower capacity tier, blunting the 4x price spike.

title: Nanotwinned-copper 150 C bonding stacks DRAM without retention loss
idea: Shift the bonding time-temperature budget down an order of magnitude: (111)-oriented nanotwinned Cu pads diffuse fast enough to bond at ~150 C in minutes, avoiding the 300-400 C anneals that degrade access-transistor leakage. DRAM can then be bonded onto finished logic without a retention penalty.
why: Protects the retention tail (fact 3) during 3D stacking, raising stack yield and trimming refresh guard bands.

title: In-package mm-wave broadcast for weight multicast
idea: MAGNIFY fan-out: on-die 140 GHz antennas let one memory chiplet broadcast the same weights to 16 compute chiplets at once, instead of 16 point-to-point copies over the interposer.
why: Data movement for inference: weight traffic falls up to 16x when chiplets share layers; removes replicated weight copies.

title: Coulomb blockade: thousand-electron charge-packet signaling read by single-electron sensors
idea: Encode each interposer bit as a ~1,000-electron charge packet clocked down a short low-capacitance line and sense it with room-temperature single-electron transistors built from sub-2 nm silicon islands whose conductance swings per elementary charge.
why: Moves ~0.16 fC per bit instead of ~40 fC (100 fF x 0.4 V): ~250x less charge, attacking pJ/bit (fact 5) at the extreme; thermal noise and reliability make it speculative.

title: Air-bridge revival: suspended interposer wires via polynorbornene thermal burnout
idea: Revive 1970s GaAs MMIC air-bridges: pattern interposer signal lines over sacrificial polynorbornene that decomposes at ~400 C and diffuses out through a thin SiN cap, leaving lines suspended in air (k~1).
why: Constraint: replaces fluorinated low-k (FSG) and HF-vapor release; wire capacitance falls ~3-4x, cutting interposer link energy ~2-3x (fact 5) and extending HBM reach.

title: Intel FIVR retreated; Sendust inductors in glass give per-channel memory DVFS
idea: Intel pulled its fully integrated voltage regulator after Haswell/Broadwell because air-core package inductors were lossy and hot, and the research magnetic inductors used banned CoZrTa. Embed laminated, sputtered Sendust (Fe-Si-Al) inductors in a glass-core substrate under each memory stack to feed per-channel buck converters in the base die, so each HBM/LPDDR channel scales VDDQ and VDD in 25 mV steps with load.
why: Voltage floor and CV2 energy (facts 5, 10): per-channel DVFS can cut I/O and array energy 20-35% during low-utilization phases; magnetics use only Fe, Si and Al.

title: Tunnel-diode Goto pairs as two-device latches in the base die
idea: Worsen: need a giant capacitor because a bit cannot hold itself. Flip: use a Goto pair (two series tunnel diodes whose N-shaped I-V curve gives two stable midpoint voltages) plus one access transistor, so each bit self-latches like SRAM with 3 devices instead of 6, built vertically in the base die.
why: Refresh-free and ~2-3x denser than SRAM; tunnel-diode peak-to-valley ratio sets standby power, which is the main risk.

title: Resonant LC tank bus recycles signal charge between complementary wires
idea: Scarcity: the whole link gets 1 pJ/bit. Pair each data wire with its complement through an on-package thin-film inductor so a transition sloshes charge from one line to the other at LC resonance (adiabatic signaling) instead of dumping CV2 to ground; drivers only top up resistive loss.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): recovering ~70-80% of line charge targets <1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM and 10-20 pJ/bit DDR5.

title: Dovetail jigsaw chiplets that self-lock edge to edge
idea: Deep-etch puzzle-tab edges on memory and logic chiplets so they interlock side by side to sub-micron accuracy, like dovetail joinery, then plate the sidewalls to form edge-to-edge links. The tiles act as a mosaic with no interposer.
why: Removes interposer cost; mm-short lateral wires cut I/O energy, using DRIE and DUV only.

title: Growth-cone interconnects: field-guided copper pillars find their pads
idea: Axon growth cones steer toward chemical cues. Here copper pillars are electrodeposited from pads on an organic panel substrate into a thin electrolyte gap, and the field from the biased pads of the chiplet above steers each growing tip so it meets its target even with several um of misalignment.
why: Capital intensity: removes high-precision bonders and silicon interposers; 5-10 um-pitch chiplet-to-substrate links on cheap organic panels with self-correcting alignment.

title: Sub-terahertz waveguides inside glass core link memory chiplets
idea: Box: HBM-lite stack x standard x standard x 300 GHz on-die patch launchers x glass-core substrate with laser-written dielectric waveguides x panel process. Instead of thousands of interposer wires, 32 sub-THz channels at 100 Gb/s each ride rectangular waveguides formed inside the package glass core, so memory can sit 20-50 mm from logic.
why: Interposer cost and shoreline: removes the 2.5D silicon interposer and decouples memory count from logic perimeter, targeting ~1 pJ/bit with 3-4x more attachable stacks.

title: Wide-slow microLED imaging-fiber links to a disaggregated memory bay
idea: Worsen: tie memory to within 5 cm of the processor so it can't be shared or cooled separately. Flip: drive hundreds of parallel microLED channels at ~2-4 Gb/s each through a coherent imaging-fiber bundle at ~0.5 pJ/bit with no DSP, so commodity DDR sits meters away in a dedicated memory bay.
why: Data movement and cost per bit: lets DDR (no 3x HBM wafer tax) feed accelerators at near-HBM energy; memory upgrades decouple from compute refreshes.

title: Approximate tensor lanes run 50 mV swing with no retries
idea: Scarcity: zero error-correction budget on the link. Tag activation and gradient traffic as approximate and run those lanes at ~50 mV swing and BER ~1e-6 with no ECC or retransmission, while pointers and metadata use standard robust lanes.
why: Interface energy and voltage floor (facts 5, 10): CV2 falls with swing, giving 3-5x lower I/O energy on most AI traffic.

title: Transit-card inductive coupling powers and talks to glued stacks
idea: Adapted from contactless smart cards: each DRAM die gets on-die spiral coils in 180 nm-era metal, used both for near-field data links and for resonant power transfer like a card reader. The dies are simply glued together, with zero TSVs and zero bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): bad dies are swapped before gluing, and there is no via-related yield loss; no DRIE or hybrid bonding needed.

title: Cool from inside: microchannels etched into memory die backsides
idea: Reverse the heat path so memory can sit on top of compute: DRIE ~100 um microchannels into the back of each die, seal them with the next bonded layer, and circulate dielectric coolant through the stack so heat leaves sideways instead of through the hot logic.
why: Removes the thermal limit on memory-on-logic stacking and HBM stack height, enabling 16+ high stacks with vertical links (facts 5, 6).

title: Decoupled access chiplet runs the address stream microseconds ahead
idea: Latency hurts only when addresses are known late, and most programs compute addresses from a small slice of their code. Compile that address slice onto a tiny access-processor chiplet that runs ~10 us ahead of the main core, issuing loads to a slow SLC-NAND or far-memory tier so data lands in a queue just in time.
why: Hides microsecond latency for irregular but computable access (graphs, sparse), so media at ~1% of DRAM price acts as working memory; trades slip penalties on data-dependent branches.

title: Royalty-free wide-slow memory interface for mature U.S. nodes
idea: Invert 'memory interfaces are written by incumbents for leading-edge PHYs': publish a federally sponsored open spec for a 2048-bit, ~2 Gb/s-per-pin unterminated memory interface that any U.S. 28-90 nm fab and glass/organic packager can build.
why: Lowers entry barriers for new U.S. memory makers and packagers; wide-slow short-reach links are cheaper and ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Congestion-charge pricing for DRAM row openings
idea: Adapted from London's congestion charge: the OS/hypervisor meters each process's row activations through memory-controller counters and charges them against a quota. Runtimes and allocators respond by restructuring data layouts for locality.
why: Overfetch and row hammer (facts 8, 9): ~20-40% fewer activations per useful bit and lower energy, with no new hardware or tools.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods with superconducting YBCO interposer wiring
idea: Po: wires have no resistance. Run memory pods at 77 K and pattern YBCO superconducting lines on the interposer, so links from many DRAM stacks to the processor are lossless over 10-100 mm, while cold DRAM retains data ~1000x longer.
why: Lossless long interposer wires allow low-swing signalling and more stacks per GPU, and cold retention nearly removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Theremin passive cavity bug revived as backscatter memory chiplets
idea: Like the 1945 Great Seal bug that transmitted with no internal power, memory chiplets carry a resonant slot antenna loaded by a varactor; the host floods the package with a 140-300 GHz carrier and reads data from the modulated reflections.
why: Fact 5: link power moves to one efficient host-side source, memory-side transmit energy <0.05 pJ/bit, and read paths need no metallurgical bond, so chiplets become wireless and easily reworked.

title: Microphase separation: block copolymer templates print 20 nm wiring on rolls
idea: Coat a block copolymer over a nanoimprinted guide pattern on R2R film; it self-assembles into 20-40 nm lamellae that template electroless metal lines, giving ultra-dense, low-cost local redistribution wiring between memory and processor.
why: Interposer wire density (fact 6) without litho tools (fact 4); large-area defectivity is the risk; local wiring only.

title: Let it rot: detect decayed lines and recompute instead
idea: Ideal: never spend energy keeping data you could regenerate. Closest achievable: KV cache and activation checkpoints sit in unrefreshed DRAM with a strong per-line checksum; when a line decays the base die flags it and the runtime recomputes it from upstream tokens or inputs instead of ever rewriting it.
why: Fact 3: zero refresh power for regenerable data, trading occasional recompute FLOPs (abundant) for retention energy and bandwidth (scarce); the leakage tail becomes a performance statistic, not a reliability wall.

title: Induction-heated bumps bond stacks without baking DRAM
idea: Substitute oven or thermocompression heating with RF induction: bumps carry a ferromagnetic nickel core that heats selectively in a 1-10 MHz field, melting solder at the joint while DRAM silicon stays below ~100 C; the tool is a coil, an RF supply and a press.
why: Retention and capital: avoids thermal stress that widens the leakage tail (Fact 3) and warpage; tool cost ~$50k.

title: Mono-material all-silicon memory package
idea: MINIFY material diversity to one: a silicon interposer, silicon lid and silicon stiffener joined by oxide-oxide and Cu-Cu bonds, with no epoxy mold, gold or solder, so the whole package is one recycling stream.
why: Recyclability and scarce resources: avoids gold, tin and tungsten chokepoints and makes silicon/copper recovery simple.

title: Compressed-sensing readout makes selector-less crossbars usable
idea: The cheapest possible cell is a two-terminal resistor at a wire crossing with no transistor or selector, but sneak paths forbid single-cell reads. Read a whole 1k x 1k tile with pseudo-random row voltage patterns, measure column currents, and let a decoder in the interface chiplet solve the linear system (with sparse coding and block parity) to recover every bit.
why: 8-16 stacked BEOL crossbar layers at 4F^2 with 2-3 masks each could approach ~100x cheaper per GB; trades latency (us tile decode), energy and endurance.

title: Jigsaw puzzle: compiler packs tensor tiles to DRAM row boundaries
idea: Like fitting jigsaw pieces: a compiler pass lays out weights and KV-cache tiles so that each row activation delivers a whole tile of useful data and every opened page is read fully, guided by the DRAM's address-mapping function.
why: Destructive read and 128x page overfetch (fact 8); cuts activation energy per useful bit 3-10x on supported workloads.

title: O: IGZO gain-cell row cache in HBM base die
idea: Add a few MB of IGZO 2T0C gain-cell memory (BEOL, seconds-scale retention, non-destructive read) on the HBM base die that caches recently opened core-die rows; repeat activations to cached rows are served from the base die with standard HBM timings, so core dies are not re-activated.
why: Destructive read/overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): fewer core activations cut internal energy ~20-30% on reuse-heavy traffic and dilute hammering, all behind the standard HBM protocol.

title: Setun balanced-ternary revival: end-to-end trits for ternary-weight models
idea: Revive the 1958 Setun balanced-ternary computer as a data path: store {-1,0,+1} weights as three charge levels (VDD/2 +/- dV) in DRAM cells, ship them over PAM-3 lanes without binary conversion, and sense them with a ternary sense amplifier.
why: Density/movement: 1.58 bits per cell versus 2-bit packing that wastes ~21%, and ternary-weight LLMs cut traffic ~10x versus FP16; end-to-end trits capture it with no unpack logic.

title: ROADM-style wavelength-addressed DRAM banks
idea: Telecom ROADMs route by color, not by address decode. Give each bank group a microring drop filter tuned to its own wavelength; the host picks the target bank by choosing a comb-laser line, so light itself routes the request and data to the bank and the global electrical decode and data bus disappear.
why: Attacks periphery (~49% of die) and global-wire energy; bank parallelism scales with comb lines (16-64) rather than with wires.

title: Time-coded analog tensor links instead of binary symbols
idea: Invert 'link symbols are digital bits': for weights and activations each wire carries a pulse whose width/edge timing encodes a 6-8-bit value, generated by a delay line and decoded by a time-to-digital converter, accepting ~1 LSB noise that AI numerics tolerate.
why: One edge pair per value instead of up to 8 bit transitions: 3-5x fewer transitions and lower CV2 on in-package links, targeting <0.5 pJ per bit-equivalent.

title: Paperclip: clip-on backside LPDDR module with pressure contacts
idea: Forced 'paperclip': a spring-clip frame presses an LPDDR module onto pads on the back of the processor substrate, directly behind the die, through compliant pogo/elastomer contacts. Traces get millimeters long, and the module stays field-replaceable.
why: I/O energy and capacity flexibility; near-PoP energy with upgradability, so less memory is overprovisioned at purchase.

title: Expose commodity DDR5 internal wide bus through one pad mask
idea: Po: the inside of the chip becomes the outside. On a standard DDR5 die, one added pad mask brings the wide internal global I/O lines up to hybrid-bond pads so a logic die bonded face-to-face reads them directly, skipping the DDR serializer and PHY.
why: Turns high-volume DDR wafers into HBM-like wide memory without TSVs or a new die design; ~3-5x lower pJ/bit than DDR5 I/O.

title: Bridge engineer's expansion joints: islands-and-meanders segmented interposer
idea: Long bridges need expansion joints: split a large interposer into rigid silicon islands, one per memory stack and logic die, joined by meandering copper-on-glass bridges that flex, so warpage and CTE stress stay small.
why: Very large memory-rich packages would otherwise warp and crack over 10 years at 125 C; this allows reticle-busting interposers carrying many more stacks.
